report:
**Conclusion:** Yes. Clinical trial evidence confirms that heavy current and former smokers who participate in regular screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) are significantly less likely to die from lung cancer.

### Key Evidence

1. **National Lung Screening Trial (NLST):** A landmark trial involving over 53,000 high-risk individuals demonstrated a 20% reduction in lung cancer mortality among participants screened annually with low-dose CT compared to those who received standard chest X-rays (https://msrads.web.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/15695/2018/08/Lung-Cancer-Screening-NEJM.pdf).
2. **NELSON Trial:** A large European randomized trial comparing volume CT screening against no screening in high-risk individuals confirmed a significant survival benefit, showing a 24% reduction in lung cancer mortality in men and a 33% reduction in women (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793, https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanres/article/PIIS2213-2600(20)30059-X/fulltext).
3. **Clinical Guidelines:** Based on these trial findings, health organizations like the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommend annual LDCT screening for eligible adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history (https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening).

By detecting lung nodules and early-stage cancers before symptoms appear, regular LDCT screening enables earlier treatment and lowers lung cancer mortality in high-risk populations.
